rules.feedback: [reviewer zai-org/GLM-5.2] The rule_context is supposed to be "informational only (no must/required/imperatives)" but it contains multiple imperative constructions that read as directives rather than standing context. For example: "Delaying the incident record pending receipt of external documentation introduces a gap in the required timeline" — "required timeline" is imperative-adjacent and the sentence functions as a directive dressed as information. More clearly: "Logging and assessment obligations are triggered at the point the staffer identifies the misdirection" states an obligation ("obligations are triggered"), which is imperative in substance. The spec says informational only, stating the general rule by criterion, not commanding action. Fix: rephrase these as criterion statements without obligation language, e.g., "The trigger point for logging and assessment is the identification of the misdirection by staff, not the receipt of external confirmation." Also, while the content is account-agnostic (no specific patient or ticket named), the level of specificity about "auto-pulled attachments that carry prior clinical data, diagnostic codes, or authorization indications containing sensitive condition markers" reads as tailored to this exact scenario rather than a general standing rule — a real standing privacy-office rule context would state the general criterion without enumerating the precise attachment types that happen to match this case. Broaden to general PHI-beyond-minimum-necessary language.

candidate.rule_context:
HIPAA wrong-recipient disclosure rule context from Meridian Privacy Office / Medical-Legal Review:

A disclosure becomes reportable when protected health information is transmitted to, or accessed by, an individual or entity outside the intended chain of custody for that specific purpose of use. The scope test is three-part: (1) the information involved is PHI as defined under 45 CFR 160.103, (2) the recipient is not the intended recipient for that specific transmission or access purpose, and (3) the disclosure was not made under a valid authorization, treatment relationship, or other applicable permission for that recipient.

Fax misdirection to an unintended business associate or external clinic meets the scope test if the information transmitted included any PHI beyond the minimum necessary for the intended referral purpose. Auto-pulled attachments that carry prior clinical data, diagnostic codes, or authorization indications containing sensitive condition markers are within scope regardless of staff intent or the cover sheet being ancillary to the main referral.

Out-of-scope: misdelivery within Meridian's own controlled systems where access is revocable and auditable; fax numbers belonging to the intended recipient but routed to a specific clinician mailbox within that entity; and purely administrative errors with no PHI content.

The risk assessment for breach notification turns on whether the unauthorized recipient actually acquired, retained, or could have retained the information, not on staff belief about recipient action. A recipient's verbal assurance of destruction without contemporaneous written certification does not negate acquisition. The absence of a written destruction certificate or similar contemporaneous documentation leaves the acquisition element unresolved in the record.

Timing of discovery does not affect reportability. A disclosure identified during the same shift is not self-resolving by prompt corrective action alone. The regulatory assessment is whether the disclosure occurred, not whether it was later remedied.

Logging and assessment obligations are triggered at the point the staffer identifies the misdirection, not at the point of receiving external confirmation. Delaying the incident record pending receipt of external documentation introduces a gap in the required timeline for risk assessment and, where applicable, the 60-day notification window under 45 CFR 164.404.

guard_nonbinding.feedback: [reviewer zai-org/GLM-5.2] The twin fails CHECK 1 (rule genuinely does not bind) because the trigger was not actually removed. The rule fires on a wrong-recipient disclosure of PHI. In the baseline, the fax auto-pulled a prior auth containing HIV status and went through to Southwest Gastro before the staffer caught it — that is the disclosure. The twin keeps the fax going through with the HIV-status prior auth attached ("the cover sheet auto-pulled the prior auth from last week... fax went through, their office confirmed receipt") and merely reframes it as authorized because Southwest Gastro is the intended GI referral recipient. But the baseline's entire premise is that Southwest Gastro IS the intended recipient — the problem was the wrong CONTENT (a prior auth with HIV status), not a wrong recipient. The how_removed even concedes the sensitive HIV indication line was transmitted: "The HIV indication line, while sensitive, was part of the existing authorized prior auth." This is a value-change inside the rule's object (same disclosure, recharacterized as authorized) while the rule keeps firing, not a genuine removal of the trigger. To fix: build a case where no PHI disclosure happens at all — e.g., the staffer catches the auto-pull BEFORE the fax goes through, or the referral cover sheet pulls nothing sensitive — so there is no transmission of the HIV-status prior auth to anyone, and the only question is the routine resend mechanics.

The HIV indication line, while sensitive, was part of the existing authorized prior auth already held by the sender and properly shareable with the receiving GI specialist for continuity of care. rules.rule_context:
HIPAA wrong-recipient disclosure rule context from Meridian Privacy Office / Medical-Legal Review:

A disclosure falls within scope when protected health information is transmitted to, or accessed by, an individual or entity outside the intended chain of custody for that specific purpose of use. The scope test is three-part: (1) the information involved is PHI as defined under 45 CFR 160.103, (2) the recipient is not the intended recipient for that specific transmission or access purpose, and (3) the disclosure was not made under a valid authorization, treatment relationship, or other applicable permission for that recipient.

Fax or electronic transmission to an unintended external recipient meets the scope test when the information transmitted included PHI beyond the minimum necessary for the intended purpose. This includes any clinical data, diagnostic information, or authorization details appended, attached, or auto-populated beyond what the intended recipient needs for that specific referral, scheduling, or routing purpose, regardless of staff intent or whether the extra information was on a cover sheet or in the body of the transmission.

Out-of-scope: misdelivery within Meridian's own controlled systems where access is revocable and auditable; routing to the correct external entity but to a specific individual mailbox within that entity; and administrative errors containing no PHI.

The risk assessment for breach notification turns on whether the unauthorized recipient actually acquired, retained, or could have retained the information, not on staff belief about recipient action. A recipient's verbal assurance of destruction without contemporaneous written certification leaves the acquisition element unresolved in the record. The absence of written documentation of destruction means the acquisition element remains active for assessment purposes.

The trigger point for logging and assessment is identification of the misdirection by staff, not receipt of external confirmation. Discovery during the same shift or prompt corrective action by staff does not remove the disclosure from scope; the occurrence of the disclosure is the criterion, not the timing of its discovery or remediation.

The 60-day notification window under 45 CFR 164.404 runs from discovery, and external documentation received after the trigger point relates to the risk assessment rather than to whether the disclosure occurred.
